title: Which of the favors?
hook: the refrain of Surah ar-Rahman: which of your Lord's favors will you deny? (Quran 55)
tomorrow: a surah named for a borrowed cooking pot? why a pot?

segments.voice: A week of two books. From the Gita: my own friend, moderate, practice and letting go. From the Quran: the opening, by time, and yesterday's morning brightness. Not forsaken.
screen: `MY OWN FRIEND · MODERATE · PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.` → `THE OPENING · BY TIME · NOT FORSAKEN.`

segments.voice: A chorus is the part everyone knows by the second time through. The Quran has a surah built around one. It opens with a single name of God, ar-Rahman, the Beneficent. Then come pictures of creation: the sun and the moon on their course, two seas that meet but don't mix, pearl and coral drawn out of them. And between the pictures, the same line keeps coming back, in Pickthall's words: "Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?"
screen: `EVERYONE KNOWS THE CHORUS.` → `SUN, MOON, TWO SEAS, PEARL.` → `WHICH OF THE FAVORS?`

segments.voice: There's a story about how to answer it. A hadith in Tirmidhi's collection says the Prophet recited this surah to his companions, start to finish, and they stayed silent. Then he told them the jinn had answered better. Each time he reached that line, they said: none of Your favors, our Lord, do we deny, and to You be praise. So the teaching is a habit of response. The refrain isn't a scolding to sit under. It's a question that wants an answer, out loud, every time it comes. Some Muslims still answer it that way when they hear the surah recited. And the twist in this story: the ones who answered well weren't the people in the room. Ar-Rahman names its favors one picture at a time, sun, sea, pearl, and after each one it stops and asks. In the hadith, the jinn answered every single one.
screen: `THE COMPANIONS STAYED SILENT.` · `THE JINN ANSWERED EVERY TIME.` · `A QUESTION THAT WANTS AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `WHICH FAVOR?`

segments.voice: Count favors on your fingers, one per finger, small and plain: a bed, a meal, a voice that called. After each one, let a short pause be your answer. When you reach ten, start over if there's time.
Which of the favors? The refrain of Surah ar-Rahman, a question that asks to be answered.
Carry this: which favor, counted out loud, one at a time. A full week: two books, seven lines.
